mainTopic: Harmful spirits, dangerous shadows, amulets, and everyday habits that cause harm (Pesachim 111b)
overview: This amud continues the גמרא's list of everyday dangers from רוחות and שדים. It opens with dangers connected to a palm tree, then lists dangerous shadows. Two general rules follow: many branches or hard wood make a shadow dangerous, with the כרו משא tree as an exception. Next the גמרא names the demons found in different places and explains that the names, and even their number, matter for writing a קמיע. Stories of a blind demon and of sixty demons in a sorb tree show these points. Then it describes the two קטב demons, tells how אביי protected a student from one, and gives the season and places where they are found. The amud ends with practical warnings from רב יוסף and others about habits that harm eyesight, bring poverty, or cause fear.

steps.title: Dangers of using a palm tree stump
steps.stepSummary: Relieving oneself on a palm stump, or resting one's head on it, brings on a harmful spirit.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone relieves himself on the stump of a cut palm tree, a פלגא spirit grabs him. If someone leans his head on the stump of a palm tree, a צרדא spirit grabs him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states two warnings about the stump of a cut palm tree. Each careless act brings a specific harmful רוח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a plain statement of danger, not an argument. The two cases share the same object, the stump of a דקל, but involve different actions, and each action brings a differently named spirit. In the translation given with the text, פלגא is a spirit of sickness, and צרדא is a spirit of headache on half the head (a migraine).

keyTerms.meaning: The stump left after a tree is cut down
A harmful spirit (also an illness caused by one)

phrases.english: One who relieves himself on the stump of a palm tree
a 'palga' spirit seizes him
phrases.notes: A 'palga' spirit is a spirit that makes a person sick.

phrases.english: And one who leans his head
on the stump of a palm tree
a 'tzerada' spirit seizes him
phrases.notes: A spirit that causes head pain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier list of dangers from spirits on this daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Relieving oneself on, or resting one's head on, a palm stump brings a harmful spirit.

steps.title: Danger of stepping over a palm tree
steps.stepSummary: One who steps over a young palm shares its fate: if it is cut or uprooted, he dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone steps over a palm tree, and the tree is later cut down, he is killed. If the tree is uprooted, he is uprooted too and dies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third palm-tree danger. Stepping over the tree ties the person's life to the tree's life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works like a linked-fate warning: what happens to the tree happens to the person. The two cases, cutting and uprooting, show that any destruction of the tree is deadly for him. The next step will limit this rule.

phrases.english: One who steps over a palm tree
if it is cut down, he is killed
if it is uprooted, he is uprooted and dies

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another palm-tree danger to the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Stepping over a palm links one's fate to the tree.

steps.title: Limit on the stepping-over danger
steps.stepSummary: The danger applies only when he steps over without placing his foot on the tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only when he did not put his foot on the tree. But if he put his foot on it, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the rule from the last step. The danger exists only if he jumps over the tree without touching it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase הני מילי signals a limit on the previous statement. The new detail is that placing a foot on the tree cancels the danger. The rule now covers only a person who passes over the tree without touching it.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply only (introduces a limit)
We have no problem with it

steps.confusionAlert: This step does not cancel the danger from step 2. It only limits that danger to stepping over without touching the tree.

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי מִילֵּי דְּלָא מַנַּח כַּרְעֵיהּ עִילָּוֵיהּ,
phrases.english: This applies only when he does not place his foot on it

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מַנַּח כַּרְעֵיהּ — עִילָּוֵיהּ לֵית לַן בַּהּ.
phrases.english: but if he places his foot on it, we have no problem with it

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי דְּלָא מַנַּח כַּרְעֵיהּ עִילָּוֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is no danger if he places his foot on the tree.

steps.title: List of dangerous shadows
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new topic: five dangerous shadows, starting with four trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are five dangerous shadows: the shadow of a single palm tree, the shadow of a כנדא tree, the shadow of a caper bush, and the shadow of a sorb tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new list of shadows that are dangerous to sit under. Four are listed here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the danger comes from a tree's shadow, not from touching the tree. Only a palm standing alone is listed, so its shadow is dangerous only when there is a single palm.
steps.confusionAlert: The heading says 'five,' but this first opinion lists only four. מפרשים offer different ways to count the five, and the next step brings an opinion that adds more.

phrases.english: There are five dangerous shadows:
the shadow of a single palm tree
the shadow of a kanda tree, the shadow of a caper bush
the shadow of a sorb tree

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from palm-tree dangers to dangerous shadows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Certain shadows are dangerous to sit under.

steps.title: Some add a ship and a willow
steps.stepSummary: Another opinion adds the shadow of a ship and the shadow of a willow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: also the shadow of a ship, and the shadow of a willow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different version of the list. This version adds two more dangerous shadows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: איכא דאמרי introduces another tradition. It keeps the original list and adds two more items to it.

phrases.english: Some say: also the shadow of a ship
and the shadow of a willow

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an expanded version of the list in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Ship and willow shadows are also dangerous, according to this opinion.

steps.title: General rule for dangerous shadows
steps.stepSummary: A shadow is dangerous if the tree has many branches or hard wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: The general rule is: anything with many branches has a dangerous shadow, and anything with hard wood has a dangerous shadow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the list into general rules. These rules let you judge trees that were not named.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate tests: many branches, or hard wood. Either one is enough to make a shadow dangerous. The next step brings an exception to the hard-wood test.

keyTerms.meaning: The general rule of the matter

phrases.english: The general rule of the matter:
whatever has many branches, its shadow is dangerous
and whatever has hard wood, its shadow is dangerous

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Generalizes the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Many branches or hard wood makes a shadow dangerous.
steps.whatToRemember: Two tests make a shadow dangerous: many branches or hard wood.

steps.title: Exception: the כרו משא tree
steps.stepSummary: כרו משא has hard wood, but its shadow is not dangerous.
steps.simpleTranslation: Except for the כרו משא tree: even though its wood is hard, its shadow is not dangerous.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives an exception to the hard-wood rule from the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hard-wood test would normally make this tree's shadow dangerous. This tree is singled out as an exception. The next step explains why.

phrases.english: except for the kero masa tree

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דִּקְשֵׁי סִילְוֵיהּ — לָא קְשֵׁי טוּלֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: even though its wood is hard, its shadow is not dangerous

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an exception to the hard-wood rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The shadow of כרו משא is not dangerous.

steps.title: The demon's warning to her son
steps.stepSummary: A demon warned her son to avoid this tree because it had killed his father. It later killed the son as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: A female demon told her son: 'Stay away from the כרו משא tree, because it killed your father.' And it later killed him too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the exception with a story. The story shows that this tree is harmful to demons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If this tree kills demons, demons stay away from it. With no demons around it, its shadow carries no danger. The ending, where the son is also killed, confirms the tree's power over them.

phrases.english: for a demon said to her son:
Keep yourself away from the kero masa tree
because it is what killed your father
and it killed him (the son) too

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the exception in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: That the shadow of כרו משא is not dangerous
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story of a demon's warning to her son

steps.title: רב כהנא avoided all shadows
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reports that he saw רב כהנא keep away from every kind of shadow.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: I saw רב כהנא staying away from all shadows.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports how one אמורא behaved in practice. He avoided all shadows, not only the ones on the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא went beyond the list and the general rules. He treated every shadow as possibly dangerous.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:

phrases.aramaic: חֲזֵינָא לְרַב כָּהֲנָא דְּפָרֵישׁ מִכּוּלְּהוּ טוּלֵּי.
phrases.english: I saw Rav Kahana keep away from all shadows

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: חֲזֵינָא לְרַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the shadow section with a report of practical behavior.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב כהנא was strict and avoided all shadows.

steps.title: Names of demons by location
steps.stepSummary: Demons have different names depending on where they are found.
steps.simpleTranslation: Demons near caper bushes are called רוחי. The one near sorb trees is called שידא. Those on roofs are called רישפי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the kinds of demons found in different places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each place has its own type of spirit, with its own name. This sets up the question in the next step: why do the names matter?

keyTerms.meaning: Spirits (the name for demons near caper bushes)
A kind of demon found on roofs

phrases.english: Those near caper bushes are 'ruchei'
the one near sorb trees is 'shida'
those on roofs are 'rishpei'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names the demons connected to some of the trees in the shadow list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each location has its own named demon.

steps.title: Why do the names matter?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference the names make.
steps.simpleTranslation: What practical difference does this make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why it needs to know these names. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Names alone seem to change nothing. The גמרא wants to know what practical use they have.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: What is the practical difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the purpose of the names in step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical use of knowing each demon's name

steps.title: The names are needed for an amulet
steps.stepSummary: The names matter for writing a קמיע.
steps.simpleTranslation: For an amulet.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a protective קמיע must name the specific demon that caused the harm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To write a קמיע for someone who was harmed, you need to know which demon to name. That is why the names have real practical value.
steps.whatToRemember: The demons' names matter because they are needed to write a קמיע.

phrases.english: For an amulet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The names are used in writing a קמיע.

steps.title: The caper-bush demon has no eyes
steps.stepSummary: The demon found by caper-bushes is a creature with no eyes.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one by the caper-bushes is a creature that has no eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a detail about the demon found near caper-bushes: it is blind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 listed the different demon names by location. Now the גמרא gives a physical description of one of them. This sets up the question that comes next: why does this detail matter?

phrases.english: The one by the caper-bushes —
is a creature that has no eyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of demons by place from step 10, now adding a description.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The caper-bush demon is blind.

steps.title: Why does it matter that it is blind?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference this detail makes.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the practical difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why we need to know that this demon has no eyes. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This uses the same question pattern as step 11. The גמרא wants every piece of information to have a real-life use.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: What is the practical difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why the detail in step 13 is useful.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical use of knowing that the demon is blind.

steps.title: You can escape it by running
steps.stepSummary: Because it cannot see, a person can flee from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: To flee from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that since the demon is blind, you can run away from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A creature that cannot see cannot follow you. So the detail tells you what to do: get away from it.

phrases.english: To flee from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Knowing it is blind tells you that you can run away from it.

steps.title: A scholar escapes the blind demon
steps.stepSummary: A young scholar fled from the caper-bush demon. It ran into a palm tree, and the demon burst.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once a young Torah scholar went to relieve himself by the caper-bushes. He heard it coming at him and fled. As the demon went, it grabbed a palm tree. The palm tree shrieked, and the demon burst.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story showing that running away from the blind demon really works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The scholar ran, and the blind demon could not follow him. Instead it crashed into a palm tree, which withered, and the demon itself burst. This supports the answer in step 15.

phrases.aramaic: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה אָזֵיל צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן
phrases.english: One time a young Torah scholar was going
to relieve himself by the caper-bushes.
He heard that it was coming at him,
and he fled from it.
As it went, it grabbed a palm tree —
the palm tree shrieked, and it burst.
phrases.notes: The palm tree withered ("shrieked"), and the demon burst.

steps.triggerLanguage: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה אָזֵיל צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story that illustrates the answer in step 15.
steps.raayaObject: That you can escape the blind caper-bush demon by fleeing.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of the young scholar by the caper-bushes.

steps.title: The sorb tree near town holds sixty demons
steps.stepSummary: The demons of the sorb tree are called שידי, and a sorb tree near a town has at least sixty of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ones by the sorb tree are called שידי. A sorb tree that is close to a town has no fewer than sixty demons.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the sorb tree. It says that a sorb tree near a town is home to at least sixty שידי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 already named the sorb-tree demon שידא. Here the plural שידי is used, and the new information is the number: sixty, when the tree is near a town.

phrases.english: The ones by the sorb tree are called שידי.
This sorb tree that is close to a town —
has no fewer than sixty demons.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the caper-bush demon to the sorb-tree demons.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sorb tree near a town holds at least sixty demons.

steps.title: Why does the number sixty matter?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference the number makes.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the practical difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why we need to know how many demons are in the tree. This sets up the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same question as before, now asked about the number sixty.

phrases.english: What is the practical difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the use of the detail in step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical use of knowing there are sixty demons.

steps.title: The number is needed for an amulet
steps.stepSummary: The number matters for writing the right קמיע.
steps.simpleTranslation: For writing an amulet for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that you must know the number of demons to write an amulet that works against them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 taught that names matter for a קמיע. Here we learn that the number matters too. An amulet against one demon will not help against sixty.

phrases.english: For writing an amulet for it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A קמיע must be written for the correct number of demons.

steps.title: An amulet for one demon fails
steps.stepSummary: Sixty demons attacked a town official. A רבי who did not know the number wrote an amulet for one demon, and the demons mocked him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain town official went and stood by a sorb tree that was close to the town. Sixty demons entered him, and he was in danger. One of the Rabbis came who did not know that it was a sorb tree of sixty demons, and he wrote an amulet against one demon. The man heard them holding a celebration inside the tree and singing: "The master's scarf is like a Torah scholar's, but we checked the master and he does not know 'ברוך'."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story showing what happens when an amulet is written for the wrong number of demons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבי's amulet covered only one demon, so it did nothing against sixty. The demons celebrated and teased him: he dresses like a scholar but does not even know the basics. This shows why step 19's point matters.
steps.confusionAlert: The demons are not really talking about a בְּרָכָה on a scarf. Their mocking song means the רבי looks like a scholar but does not know how to write an amulet properly.

phrases.english: A certain town official
who went and stood by a sorb tree
that was close to the town —
sixty demons entered him, and he was in danger.
A certain one of the Rabbis came

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא יְדַע דְּזַרְדְּתָא דְּשִׁיתִּין שֵׁידֵי הִיא,
phrases.english: who did not know it was a sorb tree of sixty demons,
and he wrote an amulet against one demon.
He heard that they were holding a celebration inside it,
and they were singing like this:
"The master's scarf is like a Torah scholar's,
but we checked the master
and he does not know 'ברוך'."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story that illustrates step 19, starting with the failed amulet.
steps.raayaObject: That an amulet must match the number of demons.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The failed amulet for one demon.

steps.title: An amulet for sixty demons works
steps.stepSummary: A רבי who knew the number wrote an amulet for sixty demons, and the demons were forced to leave.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain one of the Rabbis came who knew that the sorb tree had sixty demons. He wrote an amulet against sixty demons, and he heard them saying: "Clear your things out of here."
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with a רבי who wrote the amulet for the correct number, and it worked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the amulet matched the sixty demons. They had to pack up and leave. The two halves of the story together prove that the number matters.
steps.whatToRemember: Knowing a demon's location, name, and number is needed for a קמיע to work. An amulet for one demon fails against sixty.

phrases.english: A certain one of the Rabbis came
who knew that the sorb tree had sixty demons.
He wrote an amulet against sixty demons,
and he heard them saying:
"Clear your things out of here."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story with the successful amulet.
steps.raayaObject: That a correctly numbered amulet works.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The successful amulet for sixty demons.

steps.title: There are two kinds of קטב
steps.stepSummary: There are two קטב demons, one before noon and one after noon.
steps.simpleTranslation: קטב מרירי: there are two קטב demons. One comes before noon, and one comes after noon.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: the demon called קטב מרירי. It explains that there are actually two of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name קטב comes from a פסוק in the Torah. The גמרא divides it into two demons based on the time of day. This sets up the descriptions of each one in the next step.

phrases.english: קטב מרירי —
there are two קטב demons.
One comes before noon,
and one comes after noon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new demon topic after the sorb-tree story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are two קטב demons, divided by time of day.

steps.title: Names and signs of the two קטב demons
steps.stepSummary: The morning demon is קטב מרירי and spins in a jug of כותח. The afternoon demon is קטב ישוד צהרים and spins in a goat's horn like a sifter.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one before noon is called "קטב מרירי." It appears in a jug of כותח and spins around in it. The one after noon is called "קטב ישוד צהרים." It appears in a goat's horn and spins in it like a sifter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives each קטב demon its own name and tells where it appears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each demon gets a name from a different פסוק: קטב מרירי from the Torah, and קטב ישוד צהרים from תהלים 91:6. Each also has its own sign: a spinning motion inside a container.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two קטב demons. The morning one is קטב מרירי, seen in a jug of כותח. The afternoon one is קטב ישוד צהרים, seen in a goat's horn.

phrases.english: The one before noon is called "קטב מרירי,"
and it appears in a jug of כותח
and spins around inside it.
The one after noon is called "קטב ישוד צהרים,"
and it appears in a goat's horn
and spins inside it like a sifter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Describes each of the two demons introduced in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The morning קטב is קטב מרירי, seen in a jug of כותח. The afternoon קטב is קטב ישוד צהרים, seen in a goat's horn.

steps.title: אביי moves his students away from a demon
steps.stepSummary: While walking, אביי sees a קטב מרירי approaching from the left. He switches רב פפא to his left and moves רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע to the safer right side.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי was walking with רב פפא on his right and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע on his left. He saw a קטב מרירי coming toward his left side. So he moved רב פפא to the left and רב הונא to the right.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story showing that the קטב מרירי from the previous step is a real danger that a person can run into. אביי protects one student by moving him away from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 named the morning demon, קטב מרירי. This story shows a sage taking active steps against it. Notice that אביי shields רב הונא but places רב פפא in the line of the demon. That puzzle sets up the next question.

phrases.english: Abaye was walking along,
and Rav Pappa was walking on his right

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ מִשְּׂמָאלֵיהּ.
phrases.english: and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua on his left.
He saw a certain ketev meriri demon
coming toward his left side.
He switched Rav Pappa to his left,
phrases.notes: The left was now the exposed side.

phrases.aramaic: וּלְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְיַמִּינֵיהּ.
phrases.english: and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua to his right.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the קטב מרירי demon described in step 23.
steps.raayaObject: That the קטב מרירי is a real and present danger
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story about אביי and his students

steps.title: רב פפא asks why he was not protected
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks אביי why he was not worried about him, since he was moved to the dangerous side.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to him: What is different about me, that you were not worried for me?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא asks a sincere question about the story itself. Why was he left exposed to the demon?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Moving רב פפא to the left seems to put him in danger for no reason. The question forces אביי to explain why he treated the two students differently.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to him:
And I, what is different about me
that you were not concerned for me?

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה רב פפא אנא מאי שנא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions אביי's choice in step 24.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רב פפא was not shielded from the demon

steps.title: Your good fortune protects you
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that רב פפא's fortunate time (מזל) protects him, so he was not in real danger.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The time stands in your favor. You are fortunate, so the demon will not harm you.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers רב פפא's question. רב פפא was in a lucky, successful period of life, so the demon could not hurt him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer adds a new idea. The danger of a מזיק depends partly on a person's fortune. רב פפא was wealthy and successful, so אביי judged that only רב הונא needed protection.

keyTerms.meaning: the hour stands for you: your fortune is strong

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַתְּ שַׁעְתָּא קָיְימָא לָךְ.
phrases.english: He said to him: You, the time stands in your favor.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה את שעתא קיימא לך
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's question from step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A person whose fortune is strong is protected from the demon.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that, in the view of the גמרא, a person's מזל can affect how vulnerable they are to מזיקין.

steps.title: When the demons are found: the dates in תמוז
steps.stepSummary: From the 1st to the 16th of תמוז these demons are definitely present. After that, it is uncertain.
steps.simpleTranslation: From the first of תמוז until the sixteenth, they are certainly found. From then on, it is uncertain whether they are found or not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the season when the קטב demons are active.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sets a time frame for the danger. The first half of תמוז carries a definite risk, and the rest of the summer carries only a doubtful one.

phrases.english: From the first of Tammuz until the sixteenth of it —
they are certainly found.
From here onward —
it is uncertain whether they are found or not found.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the story, the גמרא returns to describing the קטב demons, now focusing on when they appear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The קטב demons are definitely present from 1 to 16 תמוז, and doubtfully present afterward.

steps.title: Where the demons are found: in short shadows
steps.stepSummary: These demons stay in shadows: the shadow of a small squill plant, short morning and evening shadows, and above all the shadow of a privy.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are found in the shadow of a squill plant less than a cubit tall, and in morning and evening shadows that are shorter than a cubit. Mostly they are found in the shadow of a privy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues describing the demons and lists the places where they stay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 27 gave the time, and this step gives the place. The common thread is shade, especially small shade under a cubit. The worst spot is the shadow of a בית הכסא.

keyTerms.meaning: squill, a plant often used as a boundary marker

phrases.english: And they are found in the shadow of a squill plant
that has not grown a cubit,
and in the shadows of morning and evening
that are not a cubit long,
and mainly in the shadow of a privy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the location of the demons to the time given in step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The demons stay in short shadows, mainly the shadow of a privy.
steps.whatToRemember: The קטב demons have a set season (early תמוז) and set places (short shadows, especially near a בית הכסא).

steps.title: רב יוסף: three habits that harm eyesight
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף lists three habits that weaken the eyes: combing dry hair, drinking wine that drips from the barrel, and putting shoes on wet feet.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: These three things weaken a person's eyesight: combing one's hair when it is dry, drinking dripping wine, and putting on shoes while the feet are still wet.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new list of dangerous habits. This one is about eyesight, from רב יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opens a new topic. The danger here is to health, not from demons, but it fits the larger section of practical warnings about dangerous practices.

keyTerms.meaning: weakness to the light (of the eyes): harm to eyesight

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי תְּלָת מִילֵּי יָהֵיב אַרְבּוֹנָא לִנְהוֹרָא:
phrases.english: These three things cause weakness to the light of the eyes:
one who combs his hair when it is dry,
and one who drinks wine dripping drop by drop,
and one who puts on shoes
while his foot is still wet.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב יוסף הני תלת מילי יהיב ארבונא לנהורא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from demons to a new list of harmful habits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Combing dry hair, drinking dripping wine, and wearing shoes on wet feet harm eyesight.

steps.title: Hanging food in the house brings poverty
steps.stepSummary: Hanging food in the house causes poverty, as the popular saying goes: one who hangs the basket hangs his sustenance.
steps.simpleTranslation: Hanging food in the house causes poverty. As people say: Whoever hangs up the basket hangs up his livelihood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new list, this time of household habits that bring poverty. It supports the first one with a common folk saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying is a play on the word "hang." Hanging up the bread basket is like hanging up, and so losing, your income. The proverb backs up the warning.

phrases.english: Hanging food in the house is harmful, causing poverty.
As people say:
He who hangs the basket hangs his sustenance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new list: habits that cause poverty.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hanging food in the house brings poverty.

steps.title: The warning applies only to bread
steps.stepSummary: The poverty warning applies only to hanging bread. Meat and fish are normally hung, so hanging them is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: We said this only about bread. But meat and fish are no problem, because hanging them is the normal way to store them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the rule from the previous step. Only bread is included.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern applies to unusual treatment of bread. Meat and fish are normally hung up for storage, so hanging them carries no bad sign.

phrases.english: And we said this only about bread,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בִּישְׂרָא וְכַוְורֵי — לֵית לַן בַּהּ,
phrases.english: but meat and fish — we have no problem with it,
since that is its normal way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the rule of step 30 to bread only.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only hanging bread brings poverty. Hanging meat and fish is normal and allowed.

steps.title: Bran and crumbs in the house; demons on certain nights
steps.stepSummary: Bran and bread crumbs left in the house cause poverty. On Friday nights and Tuesday nights, מזיקין rest on the crumbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Bran in the house causes poverty. Bread crumbs in the house cause poverty. On Friday nights and on Tuesday nights, harmful spirits rest on them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the poverty list with bran and crumbs. It adds that on certain nights demons settle on the crumbs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two more poverty items are added. Then the crumbs are linked back to the demon theme: on the nights when מזיקין are about (Friday night and the night before Wednesday), they rest on the crumbs.

phrases.english: Bran in the house causes poverty.
Crumbs in the house cause poverty.
On Shabbat nights and on Tuesday nights —
harmful spirits rest upon them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of poverty-causing habits begun in step 30.
steps.confusionAlert: "לילי רביעית" means the night that begins Wednesday, which is Tuesday night, because the Jewish day starts at nightfall. It does not mean Wednesday night.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bran and crumbs in the house bring poverty, and on Friday and Tuesday nights מזיקין rest on the crumbs.
steps.whatToRemember: Avoid hanging bread, leaving bran, and leaving crumbs in the house, since these bring poverty. Crumbs also attract מזיקין on Friday and Tuesday nights.

steps.title: The names of the angels over food and over poverty
steps.stepSummary: The angel in charge of food is called נקיד, meaning clean. The angel in charge of poverty is called נבל, meaning disgraceful.
steps.simpleTranslation: The angel appointed over food is named נקיד, because he is clean. The angel appointed over poverty is named נבל, because he is disgraceful.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the names of two angels. One is in charge of food and the other is in charge of poverty. This explains the last step, where leftover crumbs in the house cause poverty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The food angel's name, נקיד, comes from נקי, which means clean. He stays away from a dirty house. The poverty angel, נבל, is at home in a messy house. So crumbs and bran left lying around push away the food angel and invite the poverty angel.

keyTerms.meaning: An appointed angel or officer in charge of something (some render it 'administering angel')
Name of the food angel; related to נָקִי, clean
Name of the poverty angel; means disgraceful or vile

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives the reason behind the last step's warning about crumbs. Poverty comes from dirtiness because the food angel avoids it.

phrases.english: The appointed angel of food
his name is 'Nakid' (clean).
The appointed angel of poverty
his name is 'Naval' (disgraceful).
phrases.notes: He thrives in a dirty place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why crumbs and bran in the house cause poverty (Step 32).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The food angel (נקיד) loves cleanliness, and the poverty angel (נבל) thrives in dirt.

steps.title: A plate placed on a jug causes poverty
steps.stepSummary: Covering a jug's opening with a plate brings poverty.
steps.simpleTranslation: A plate placed on the mouth of a jug is harmful, because it causes poverty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another habit that brings poverty: putting a plate on top of a jug.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the list of household habits that lead to poverty, after hanging bread and leaving crumbs. The phrase קשי לעניותא, 'is harmful for poverty,' means the habit causes poverty. The same phrase pattern is used again in the next step for a different harm.

phrases.english: A plate on the mouth of a jug —
is harmful, causing poverty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another poverty-causing habit to the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Placing a plate over a jug causes poverty.

steps.title: Drinking water from a plate harms the eyes
steps.stepSummary: Drinking water out of a plate causes an eye illness.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who drinks water from plates harms himself by bringing on an eye illness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from poverty to a health warning. Drinking water from a plate causes an eye problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same formula, קשי ל, is used here, but now the harm is to the body and not to wealth. The illness is called ברוקתי, which is an eye disease. It links back to the list of eye-weakening habits in Step 29.
steps.confusionAlert: The same phrase 'קשי ל' appears in both warnings. In Step 34 it means 'causes poverty,' and here it means 'causes an eye illness.' Don't carry the poverty meaning into this line.

phrases.english: One who drinks water from plates —
it is harmful, causing an eye illness.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּשָׁתֵי מַיָּא בְּצָעֵי קְשֵׁי לִבְרוּקְתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same 'plate' theme and formula as Step 34, but warns about a health harm instead of poverty.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Drinking water from a plate causes an eye illness.

steps.title: Eating cress without washing hands brings thirty days of fear
steps.stepSummary: Someone who eats cress and does not wash his hands afterward will be afraid for thirty days.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who eats cress and does not wash his hands will be frightened for thirty days.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more warning about a dangerous habit: eating cress without washing your hands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the harm is fear, not poverty or illness. The גמרא states the result, thirty days of fear, without giving a reason. It is one more item in the list of everyday habits that carry a hidden harm.
steps.whatToRemember: This part of the daf lists everyday habits and their harms. Dirt and carelessness bring poverty (the food angel נקיד loves cleanliness). Other habits bring eye illness or fear.

phrases.english: One who eats cress
and does not wash his hands —
will be afraid for thirty days.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָכֵיל תַּחְלֵי וְלָא מָשֵׁי יְדֵיהּ מְפַחֵיד תְּלָתִין יוֹמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another harmful habit; here the harm is fear rather than poverty or eye illness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating cress without washing hands afterward brings thirty days of fear.
